newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Tribunal calls on NZ govt to repair treaty breaches.
newsitem.headline: Tribunal calls on NZ govt to repair treaty breaches.

text.p: A New Zealand tribunal said on Wednesday that northern Maori tribes were justified in claims that the government breach of historic treaty obligations had far-reaching social and economic consequences.

The Waitangi Tribunal, set up to consider breaches of the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi between Maori and European settlers, said reparation options could include the return of a huge tract of land including valuable government-owned plantation forests.

The tribunal, which has the power to make a mandatory order, also suggested financial compensation and the payment of other state assets to rectify "profound social and economic consequences" resulting in physical deprivation, poverty, social dislocation and loss of status.

Maori, who make up about 13 percent of New Zealand's 3.6 million people, are overrepresented in poor health, unemployment, poverty and crime figures with those in the far north among the worst affected.
The report is sure to stir up controversy.
Treaty Negotiations Minister Doug Graham and Treasurer Winston Peters said earlier in the week that the government could not afford to return all the forests.
"Such a settlement, if spread over other settlements on a pro-rata basis, would bankrupt the country," Peters, himself a Maori from the far north, said on Monday.

The government has recently settled several significant Maori claims including one with Waikato tribes in the central North Island for NZ$170 million (US$118 million) and one with the main South Island tribe, Ngai Tahu, for a similar amount.
Graham welcomed the report but expressed hope that claimants, known as the Muriwhenua, would present a unified claim to negotiate directly with the government.
"The Tribunal comments that Treaty breaches led to the district having one of the worst records of Maori social and economic disadvantage," Graham said.
Race relations in New Zealand, historically good by international standards and improving in recent years, have been upset by two developments this month.
A Maori activist is accused of criminal damage after a sledgehammer attack on the prestigious America's Cup yachting trophy, won by New Zealand in 1995.
Some white New Zealanders are also up in arms over a judge's ruling that Maori, thanks to their traditional rights to land and rivers, do not need a licence to fish for trout in some circumstances.
The six Muriwhenua claimants claim 170,000 hectares (420,000 acres) of land, including popular tourism spots.

Graham said it would be "undesirable" for the tribunal to make a binding ruling on the government. "The effect of that order, if they do make one, might have repercussions that are far reaching," he said.
The tribunal said settlement of the grievance was urgent.

"These matters of consequential impacts in terms of land tenure reform and disempowerment, and the serious social and economic conditions that still prevail in Muriwhenua, underline the need for early relief," the tribunal said.
